clue.text: Gone With the Wind?

blocks.note: surface reading: the title of the famous novel and film
setter's reading: carried along by moving air, as a boat or leaf is

explanation.walkthrough: The capitals dress it up as the Margaret Mitchell title; read literally, something that has gone with the wind has floated off on it.
explanation.definitionFit: To drift is to be carried along by a current of air or water, so whatever went with the wind did this.

clue.text: Slander half-deaf celebrity

indicators.note: only half of the following word is kept, so the rest of its letters are dropped

blocks.note: taken as written before halving
celebrity is renown

explanation.surface: Someone badmouths a famous person who is partly deaf.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half of DEAF is DE; add FAME for DEFAME.
explanation.definitionFit: Both verbs mean to damage someone's reputation with false statements.

clue.text: Break in and sound pleased about smashing something

indicators.note: turned about means facing the other way, so the word is read backwards
smashing into something means breaking inside it, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: a cat sounds pleased by purring
it stands for an unnamed thing

explanation.surface: A burglar breaks in, gleefully smashing things as they go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smashing' reads as destruction in the surface, but here it just means pushing into the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: To irrupt is to burst or force one's way into a place, which is breaking in.

clue.text: The corps not here? I sympathise

blocks.note: taken as written
the Royal Engineers, a British Army corps
the opposite of here

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether the troops are missing, then offers comfort.
explanation.walkthrough: RE is the Royal Engineers, the British Army's engineering corps.
explanation.definitionFit: 'There, there' is the soothing phrase said to comfort someone upset, expressing sympathy.

clue.text: Wise daughter looking up French artist

indicators.note: in a down entry, looking up means the word runs from bottom to top

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for daughter
a sage is wise

explanation.surface: A clever girl gazes up at a painting by a French master.
explanation.definitionFit: Edgar Degas was the French Impressionist painter known for his ballet dancers.

clue.text: Public library ticket includes a notice

indicators.note: to include something is to hold it within, so a piece goes inside the phrase before

blocks.note: abbreviation for public library
a card can serve as a ticket
taken as written

explanation.surface: A library card comes with an attached notice.
explanation.definitionFit: A placard is a sign or poster displaying a public notice.

clue.text: Depiction of grand entrance pierced by a little sunshine

indicators.note: something pierced has another thing pushed into it, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: a portal is an imposing doorway
a ray is a small beam of sunlight

explanation.surface: A painting shows a stately doorway with a shaft of sunlight through it.
explanation.definitionFit: A portrayal is a representation of someone or something in art or words, a depiction.

clue.text: A container not properly closed

blocks.note: taken as written
a jar is a container

explanation.surface: A lid has been left loose on some receptacle.
explanation.definitionFit: A door left ajar is slightly open, so not fully shut.

clue.text: As is lithe cat, racing around?

definitions.text: As is lithe cat, racing around?

indicators.note: something racing around is in wild motion, so the letters run about into a new order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A supple cat dashing about shows a sporty nature.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: a lithe cat racing around is exactly what the answer describes.
explanation.definitionFit: A supple animal sprinting about is fit and agile, which is being athletic.

clue.text: Come rapidly down to earth with a bang

definitions.text: Come rapidly down to earth with a bang

blocks.note: surface reading: someone falling or being brought quickly back to reality
setter's reading: an aircraft plunging steeply to drop explosives

explanation.walkthrough: 'Come down to earth with a bang' sounds like a sudden disillusionment; read literally it is a warplane's steep attack.
explanation.definitionFit: To dive-bomb is to swoop steeply on a target and release a bomb near the ground.

clue.text: A long way to church, a ridiculous situation

blocks.note: far means a long way off
Church of England

explanation.surface: Having to travel miles to church becomes a ridiculous ordeal.
explanation.definitionFit: A farce is an absurd, chaotic state of affairs, like the comic stage genre.

clue.text: Important Russian composer covered in blood, see

indicators.note: something covered in a substance is wrapped by it, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: J S Bach, the German composer
gore is spilt blood
v is short for vide, Latin for see

explanation.surface: A notable Russian composer is found bloodied; look.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Important Russian' seems to describe the composer, but it is the definition; the composer is German.
explanation.definitionFit: Mikhail Gorbachev, last leader of the Soviet Union, was a figure of great historical importance.

clue.text: A supremely awful 'Don't mention it!'

indicators.note: something awful is a mess, so the letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone brushes off thanks in a dreadfully grand manner.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are polite replies to thanks, saying the favour was no trouble at all.

clue.text: Say Rosemary is in another building

indicators.note: the answer is said to sit inside the next words, lying across their letters

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of one word and start of the next

explanation.surface: A woman named Rosemary has moved into a different building.
explanation.walkthrough: Rosemary looks like a woman's name; 'say' marks it as an example of a plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Rosemary is an aromatic plant used in cooking, an example of a herb.

clue.text: Wait a bit: I haven't left Paddington

blocks.note: first meaning: a request for patience
second meaning: the famous bear is still in my company

explanation.walkthrough: Paddington looks like the London railway station; it is Paddington Bear, the children's-book bear, still beside the speaker.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase asks for patience, and literally says the bear is still alongside me.

clue.text: One result of successful seance, nothing extreme?

blocks.note: first meaning: a spiritualist pleased that contact was made
second meaning: a balanced middle course

explanation.walkthrough: The first meaning reads the stock phrase literally as a contented psychic.
explanation.definitionFit: A happy medium is a sensible compromise between extremes, and also a cheerful clairvoyant.

clue.text: Such a nasty letter from Post Office, with wrong pension

indicators.note: something wrong is not in its proper state, so the letters are set out differently

blocks.note: standard abbreviation
the letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A pensioner gets an angry letter from the Post Office over a payment error.
explanation.definitionFit: A poison-pen letter is an anonymous malicious one, so the answer describes such a nasty letter.

clue.text: Cancelled, not without a fight?

blocks.note: first meaning: called off or abandoned
second meaning: fought, since a scrap is a fight

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests something called off only after a struggle; the second half means having had a scrap, informal for a brawl.
explanation.definitionFit: Scrapped means abandoned as a plan, and also brawled, as scrap is slang for fight.

clue.text: Poet isn't working: hurry up!

indicators.note: letters set working are put into action and moved around into a new order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An idle poet is told to get a move on.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Step on it' is an idiom from pressing the accelerator, meaning go faster.

clue.text: Provide food at a sort of box for young peacock

blocks.note: to cater is to supply meals
a pillar box is a British red street postbox

explanation.surface: Catering for a young peacock at some kind of box sounds like feeding a chick.
explanation.walkthrough: The peacock is the peacock butterfly, not the bird; its young is a larva.
explanation.definitionFit: The peacock is also a butterfly, and a butterfly's larval stage is a caterpillar.

clue.text: Quietly tramps to see the moon

blocks.note: p is piano, musical notation for quietly
hobos are vagrants

explanation.surface: Vagrants creep along silently to look at the moon.
explanation.definitionFit: Phobos is the larger of the two natural satellites of Mars.

clue.text: For heavyweight, a tiny scrap

blocks.note: pro means in favour of
a ton is a large weight

explanation.surface: A tiny bout is set up for a heavyweight boxer.
explanation.walkthrough: Scrap looks like a fight, as befits a heavyweight; here it means a minute particle.
explanation.definitionFit: A proton is a subatomic particle, an extremely small bit of matter.

clue.text: An elected member's current measures

blocks.note: an is the indefinite article, a
Member of Parliament
taken as written

explanation.surface: A politician's present-day policies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' looks like present-day; it is electric current.
explanation.definitionFit: Amps are units measuring electric current.

clue.text: Seductive, appear to have success with woman

blocks.note: to come is to turn up
a hit is a success
the female pronoun

explanation.surface: An alluring person seems to score with a woman.
explanation.definitionFit: A come-hither look is one that invites and entices, so it is flirtatiously alluring.

clue.text: Choose from the lectionary

indicators.note: the answer is taken out of the following words, lying inside them

blocks.note: the letters span the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: Pick a reading from the church's book of scripture passages.
explanation.walkthrough: A lectionary is a book of Bible readings for church services.
explanation.definitionFit: To elect is to pick by vote or decision, so it means to select.

clue.text: Father appearing twice a year

blocks.note: pa is per annum, a year, written two times

explanation.surface: Dad visits only twice annually.
explanation.definitionFit: Papa is an affectionate word for one's dad.

clue.text: Long to take one fruit or another

definitions.note: stands for another fruit, as the clue has just named one

blocks.note: to pine is to yearn
the apple is a fruit

explanation.surface: Someone yearns to pick a piece of fruit, any will do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fruit' looks like the definition, but it belongs to the wordplay; the answer is defined by 'another', meaning a second fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: The pineapple is a tropical fruit, a different one from the apple named in the wordplay.

clue.text: Hospital has not much custom

blocks.note: H is the map symbol for hospital
a bit is a small amount

explanation.surface: A hospital sees few patients these days.
explanation.definitionFit: A habit is a regular practice or routine, a custom.

clue.text: Step on to platform and run into arrest

indicators.note: one piece goes into the other, so it is placed inside it

blocks.note: to detain is to hold in custody
R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: A fugitive gets off and runs straight into the police.
explanation.definitionFit: To detrain is to get off a train, stepping out onto the station platform.

clue.text: Acts of disloyalty aren't so bad

definitions.note: plural phrase; the answer is a mass noun covering such acts

indicators.note: letters gone bad are spoiled, so their order is broken and rebuilt

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone insists that betrayals are really not so terrible.
explanation.definitionFit: Treason is betrayal of one's country or sovereign, the gravest kind of disloyal conduct.
